title: Art and design schools must act as a system, not a market
summary: Zey Suka-Bill and Christoph Lindner argue art and design universities' real opportunity lies in collaboration and partnerships
full_text:
For decades, specialist art and design universities in the United Kingdom have operated within a model shaped largely by competition.

Despite a shared role in shaping the UK’s world-leading creative sector, we compete for students, funding, visibility, and position in an increasingly complex global landscape.

However, demographic change, financial pressure, technological innovation, and intensifying global competition are now placing new demands on specialist institutions that, at their foundation, were not designed to operate in isolation.

In this context, competition remains important for enabling student choice, but no longer works as the primary organising principle. Left unchecked, competition leads to fragmentation, duplication, and a less coherent sector than the one we collectively need.

The effects are already visible.

Students navigate a confusing educational landscape which particularly disadvantages those without family experience of understanding their options. This is especially true if they are moving between institutions, often without clear articulation of how their learning connects or progresses.

Art and design universities, as with the higher education sector more broadly, invest in parallel responses to shared challenges, from curriculum redesign to digital transformation. Nationally, the voice of creative education is less coordinated at a moment when the entire arts ecosystem is under extreme pressure, and changes to specialist institution funding loom on the horizon.

As the world around us changes, so too must the way institutions organise themselves. A gradual rebalancing is now emerging: a recognition that competition works best when it sits alongside deliberate forms of cooperation. This invites a shift in both perspective and behaviour, from a sector that acts primarily as a market to one that can also act as a system.

Cooperation, in this sense, does not diminish institutional identity. Instead, it builds on the distinctiveness of UK art and design education – precisely what gives it global strength – by enabling institutional differences to complement one another, and create a more connected and legible landscape for students, staff, and partners.

Step on up

At the Royal College of Art (RCA), we have been in dialogue with a growing group of art and design institutions in the UK and Ireland, asking ourselves the question: how could we build a shared future differently?

The most immediate opportunity lies in student pathways. Art and design excellence continues to be widely distributed across the country, but access – particularly at postgraduate level – is not.

This higher level study is crucial to creating the art and design leaders of tomorrow, and driving nationwide growth in the creative industries – yet currently students encounter a lack of continuity between undergraduate and postgraduate study, including structural, financial, and curricular blocks. This constrains progression, not through lack of ability, but through lack of clarity, which in turn limits access. A more cooperative approach can help address this.

This is why the RCA has begun building a network of partnerships with a growing number of specialist art and design institutions across the UK and Ireland. Together, we are developing structured progression routes in disciplines vital to the continued success of our creative industries, such as fashion, animation, moving image, product design, graphic communication, and digital arts. These are academically aligned and in key areas both for graduate careers and for the growth of the creative sector. Crucially, this approach maintains institutional standards while offering students clearer, faster routes into advanced study.

This approach also enables us to create a more connected ecosystem between institutions for curriculum development, teaching innovation, and addressing the urgent questions shaping the creative industries and our world.

Creative and critical enquiry into artificial intelligence, sustainability, equity, and the future of creative work are not confined to individual institutions – yet they are still often addressed independently.

In a resource-constrained environment, sharing is not a compromise. It is a way of strengthening the sector’s capacity to seize opportunities, build resilience, and maximise impact.

Cooperation over duplication

And the same applies to research and doctoral education in art and design.

While the UK has considerable strength in practice-based research, capacity is unevenly distributed. Here, cooperation offers a practical alternative to duplication. Co-supervised doctoral projects, shared training provision, and collaborative research projects are already beginning to take shape.

One example is Ecological Citizen(s), a four-year Network+ project based at the RCA in collaboration with the University of York’s Stockholm Environment Institute and Wrexham University, which brings design research, environmental expertise, and civic engagement together to support positive climate action in a digital society.

Collaboration has long been part of higher education, but the current context invites a more deliberate and structured engagement with it. This is not without complexity. Collaboration requires trust, purpose, and careful attention to standards, autonomy, and resources. It also takes time. But the direction of travel is becoming clearer, as more art and design institutions look for ways to respond collectively to shared pressures and opportunities.

Healthy competition will remain part of this landscape.

The opportunity now is to strengthen relationships and drive a more coordinated approach to the future, where collaboration is not occasional, but structurally embedded in how the sector operates. This is vital both to support the widest possible range of students, and to ensure that the talent pipeline into our creative industries continues to be strong.

In doing so, UK art and design education can retain its world-renowned distinctiveness while responding more quickly and adeptly to change.

title: A fresh cost of living crisis is coming for students. You’d never know
summary: With OfS's proposed fairness condition under consultation, Jim Dickinson audits what universities tell applicants about costs – and finds silence, archaeology or arithmetic that doesn't add up
full_text:
Food prices in the UK have risen by around 39 per cent since January 2020.

Higher energy and agricultural commodity prices have combined with rising labour costs, new regulatory burdens, supply-chain disruption and the structure of the food market to increase costs throughout the system.

These pressures move gradually from farms and energy suppliers through manufacturers, distributors and retailers before appearing in the prices paid by consumers.

The Food and Drink Federation argues that the industry is now less able to absorb another major shock after five years of cost-cutting and attempts to extract efficiencies from supply chains and operations.

The war in Iran has therefore appeared at a point of reduced resilience, with disruption to Middle Eastern energy production and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz threatening another sharp rise in energy and transport costs.

As a result, the federation has substantially increased its forecast for UK food inflation. Having previously expected inflation of 3.2 per cent, it now predicts that annual food price inflation will reach between 9 and 10 per cent by December 2026.

On that basis, analysis from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit puts UK food prices on track to be 50 per cent higher by November 2026 than at the start of the cost of living crisis in mid-2021 – squeezing almost two decades’ worth of pre-crisis price growth into a little over five years, with staples like pasta, frozen vegetables, eggs and beef all up by more than half.

And the shock hasn’t fully arrived yet. Britain is heading for its worst cereal harvest since records began in 1984, drought and heat have pushed wholesale tomato prices up more than 60 per cent and potatoes more than 40 per cent just as the same weather hits the European suppliers we’d normally import from, and the FAO reckons commodity cost rises take three to six months to reach retail prices – landing them squarely in autumn and winter.

Food price inflation is always higher for those who mainly buy own brands or raw materials – a venn diagram that has students all over it. Meanwhile the latest energy price cap change, on 1 July 2026, was a 13 per cent increase – which we’d have to assume nobody has noticed given the heatwave.

For some years now landlords offering “all inclusive bills” have been advised to bury acceptable use caps into those contracts, in pounds and pence rather than unit costs, to protect against price shocks. Of the sort we’ll experience this winter.

A student’s basket of goods is more heavily dominated by food, and if they rent, energy costs. HM Treasury has gathered expert estimates for average family CPI of between 3.1 to 4.5 per cent this autumn, in a year when the Department for Education has “future proofed” maximum maintenance loans to go up by 2.7 per cent.

That’s the max of course – thanks to that frozen means testing threshold, the median maintenance loan for a full-time student is projected by DfE to go up by 1.2 per cent this September.

In the face of all of that, we might have expected the sector’s cost of living information for prospective students to have improved beyond the shower I’ve found in previous summers (2025, 2024, 2024b, 2023, 2022).

Sadly, if anything, it’s the worst I’ve seen.

The archaeology

On the website of one institution in London, in a document explaining living costs to prospective US federal loan borrowers, accommodation was last revised in “Feb 2014”. Utilities, food and travel in “May 2013”. Entertainment in “December 2013”. Students weighing up a five-figure dollar loan in 2026 are told food costs £63 a week, on the authority of a spreadsheet that predates the 2015 general election.

One Scottish university publishes a full itemised budget marked “Living costs are approximate – May 2023”, advising that a rented flat in its home city costs £600 a month. That city is Edinburgh, where UCAS/BlackBullion reckon the real range is £574 – £1,386 a month.

An institution in London tells applicants that living in the capital “is likely to cost £1,300 to £1,550 a month” – the exact figure it quoted in May 2022 – on a page where the tuition fees, helpfully, are bang up to date for 2026/27.

Another institution tells its overwhelmingly international postgraduate intake to budget for warm clothing at 2020 prices, travel at 2020 prices, and utilities on “2023 data” – the page hasn’t been touched since I flagged it two years ago.

And one London university has pioneered what we might call de-labelling. Last year its international costs page marked its monthly ranges “2023/24”; this year that page is gone – the URL now redirects to a rebuilt finance page serving the identical ranges and example prices with the year label removed. Its student travelcard rate is a fare revision behind too – the rebuilt page’s visa costs are current and correct, the rest not so much.

Special mention to one Welsh university, whose international costs page discloses “Page last updated 17.08.23” above figures built on crowd-sourced data from that same August, “with a slight adjustment… to account for inflation over the next few months”… of 2023. The page also warns, in the present tense, that costs are rising “at the moment”.

One North West institution’s entire cost hub brags it has the “lowest cost of living in the UK”, based on a 2023 newspaper ranking, Save the Student 2023, and a TV licence at £13.25 a month (the 2021–23 rate in monthly disguise).

One Scottish institution’s international costs table – framed for 2025/26, prices the TV licence at £13.25 a month, which is the £159 annual rate abolished in 2024, meaning the figure was already two years stale on the day the page was framed.

Another Scottish institution offers “£1,104 a month” on the authority of a 2024 survey, alongside utility ranges of “£0–200” – a span that includes both freezing to death and not having a boiler. It’s been bothered to update its own rent figures and TV license costs since last year, but none of the others.

One northern university’s international page prices bowling “with NUS card” – a card retired in 2019 – on a page whose other figures are identical to those published in 2023. A note at the foot says the university “makes every effort to ensure that the information published on this page is accurate”, a note which appears to confuse the word “every” with “little”.

A fresh coat of paint

A page that says when it was last updated sounds like good practice, but in many cases the sector has responded by discovering that you can update the date without updating the page.

One university in the North West carries a May 2026 modification stamp in its page metadata. Every single “expect to pay at least” figure on it – shopping £170 a month, bills £80, going out £55, eating out £30, self-care £30, the lot – is identical to the August 2024 archive capture, down to a stray space in a typo (“Expect to pay at least : £33 a month”).

One institution’s living costs calculator presents “estimates for 2026/27” – and against the August 2025 capture, which presented “estimates for 2025/26”, every figure is identical to the penny – £1,216.93 a month, £10,952.40 a year. The same page quotes “the minimum cost of living as recommended by UKVI” at £1,023 a month – two upratings expired, and not a cost of living recommendation even when it was alive.

A Scottish university advised students that living in the city costs “£1,100 to £1,700 per month to live and study… published May 2024”. This year it estimates “£1,100 to £1,700 per month to live and study…based on a small sample survey of current students”. What are the chances!

A business school in the capital opts for consistency over relabelling – its Masters cost-of-living ranges for utilities, travel, food and entertainment are identical for the third consecutive year – 2024 capture, 2025 article, 2026 live – which for an institution that teaches forecasting is either negligence or a very strong view on inflation.

One provider’s weekly guide is stamped “estimated as of April 2025”. Against the March 2021 capture, exactly three of its ten lines have ever changed. Entertainment, travel, books, broadband, “other costs”, contents insurance and a TV licence priced at “£1” a week are all serving their sixth year. That £1, incidentally, is the abolished 2021–23 licence fee divided by three housemates and 52 weeks – a stale statutory rate laundered through a per-person share.

We’ve updated the prices. Ours.

The most reliable finding across 141 providers is that where a page has been partially updated, the parts that moved are the prices the university charges, and the parts that didn’t are the costs the student bears everywhere else.

One university’s affordability page has opened with the same sentence since October 2022 – students “can spend around £475 per week on rent and living costs”. The component ranges under it have quietly crept up – rent £120–290 then, £180–300 now; food £30–40 then, £50–80 now – except contents insurance (£1.50–£2.50) and the clothing-and-going-out line (£40–130), unchanged to the penny across four years of inflation. Nothing on the page is sourced.

Another institution has repriced its accommodation repeatedly – £158–337 a week last year, £183–408.50 now – while its food estimate (£30 to £40 a week) and entertainment (£20 to £50) enter year six unchanged, with utility bills listed, in full, as “variable”.

Another university has advised £80 a month for utilities since 2018 – a figure that has survived the entire European energy crisis without flinching – on a page stamped “correct July 2025”; against the July 2024 capture, exactly two lines have moved – the visa figure and the campus nursery price. And its one-off-costs boilerplate (£1,000 laptop, £400–450 winter clothing, £500 for trips) is word-for-word identical to a Midlands university’s page. Even the errors are copy-pasted.

The long-service award goes to a post-92 first I first looked at in 2022, when nothing on its costs page had changed since 2015 except its own halls prices. The May 2024 capture against today’s page extends the streak – every row identical except accommodation. Its “£45 weekly” bus pass and “£20–£100 weekly” phone costs – figures that are self-evidently monthly-scale, sitting in a weekly column – have now survived a decade of “updates” unexamined.

On the south coast, a university whose costs are “based on sector averages… monitored by our Student Money team” has nudged rent and food since the 2024 capture while travel, phone, social costs and a £3-a-week TV licence run unchanged since at least 2020 – and the caveat about “rapidly rising energy costs” that used to sit on the page has been quietly deleted. Bills have somehow got… cheaper!

At one university, since its April 2024 capture, the single students’ lines have all been repriced, but the family totals – couple £2,750 a month, couple with one child £3,000 – are frozen even though the accommodation components inside them went up. The totals no longer sum. Someone updated the ingredients and declined to update the cake.

And back in Wales, an itemised page carries its own domestic contradiction – introductory text advising a “maximum target of £80 per week” for a private room, directly above a table pricing that room at £110.

The incredible shrinking food shop

As I note above, food inflation is forecast to hit nine to ten per cent by the end of this year, per the Food and Drink Federation. Four universities have responded by cutting their food estimates.

One in the South West publishes a properly dated, itemised sample budget as a PDF, filed under its corporate publications section where no applicant will ever trip over it. Set this year’s edition against its own still-live 2024–25 edition and the food line has gone from £69 a week to £50. Rent rose from £169 to £183 and utilities from £24 to £41, so the headline total moved just £11. The food line, it turns out, is a shock absorber – it exists to soak up the rises in the numbers the university controls so the total stays presentable.

One university managed, in a May 2026 refresh, to cut food from £70 a week to £50 and course essentials from £20 to £5, while nudging “other – additional leisure, sport, hobbies and socialising” up from £80 to £100 and repricing its own accommodation upward. Students will eat less, buy no books, and have a lovely time.

In the South West, one university’s example budget prices a TV licence at “£3.30 a month” – the abolished £159 annual fee split across a four-bed house, a fossil hidden inside a fraction – and its non-rent budget was cut by around a fifth between the March 2023 capture and today while the rent line rose by up to half.

One London institution’s catered-accommodation budget for international students includes a food line of £40 – a month. Catering covers term-time weekday meals, but £1.30 a day for every other meal a human eats feels like a stretch in London.

Out of 141 providers, the number that tell prospective students that costs will rise materially during their course – with food inflation heading for double digits, hardly a niche prediction – is two. Both are ancient, both are rich.

One advises applicants to “allow for potential increases in living expenses of around 4% each year”, from figures built on a joint survey with its own students’ union blended with the government’s income and expenditure research, the other adjusts its published figures using the Bank of England’s inflation forecast. The universities with the least worried applicants provide the most honest forecasts. Everyone else presents this year’s prices (or 2021’s) as though the future has been cancelled.

Out of date, out of pocket

If there is one number a university has no excuse for getting wrong, it is the Home Office maintenance requirement – a figure with a statutory value, a publication date and a gov.uk page. Here is how that’s going.

Several providers still quote £9,207 – the requirement that expired in 2021. One prints its provenance with archaeological care – “from December 1st 2020 the minimum requirement for your living costs is £9,207”, on a US federal aid page that also quotes an NHS surcharge of £470 (the rate that ended in October 2020; it is now £776) and a visa fee of £350 (now £524). Every regulated number on the page predates the end of the pandemic.

Another publishes the £9,207 in English and in Welsh, on a postgraduate FAQ last touched in September 2023 – a bilingual commitment to misinformation. An applicant who takes that page at its word will evidence £1,332 less than the real requirement, and their visa will be refused.

One Midlands university quotes the requirement as “£1,203 per month”. No such rate has ever existed – the sequence runs £1,015, £1,023, £1,136, £1,171. It appears to be a typo of £1,023 that nobody has noticed since the page was “Last updated: 16/08/2024”, a stamp it has worn through a September 2025 archive capture and into the present day.

A Yorkshire institution describes £1,023 a month as what “UK Visas and Immigration consider… a reasonable budget for an international student in Britain” – present tense, eighteen months after the rate expired, and even when it was current it was a visa threshold, not a budget. Its April 2025 capture shows the same sentence, so it spent that spring calling an expired rate “reasonable” too.

One Welsh institution has a page for international students titled “Estimated Costs of Living” – and the only estimate on it is the visa proof-of-funds figure, presented as what students should “budget to have”. Its recommended external tool for working out living costs (“student calculator”) links to a payday loans operator. The only cost of attendance document a US borrower can find on the site is a PDF from May 2020, quoting visa costs at less than half current rates.

In London, one university quotes £1,483 – one uprating behind – while a midlands institution quotes the current rate and then advises Master’s students to plan “£13,632 for a full year” – which is twelve times the expired £1,136; the right instinct, wearing last year’s arithmetic.

And a London provider has the current £1,529, which it presents as the amount students need “to meet basic living expenses” – an evidential threshold repackaged as a lifestyle guide, on a page where the food, campus meal and heating figures date from 2021.

Ask twice, get three answers

A special category for universities disagreeing with themselves in public.

One London institution currently offers three simultaneous answers to “how much will I need?”. Its domestic pages say £17,000 to £21,800 a year. Its international fees page says £12,000 to £13,000 will “cover living costs for one calendar year”. Its US cost of attendance filing says £25,486 for 42 weeks, or £31,554 for 52. The cheapest answer is shown to international applicants; the most expensive to the US Department of Education, which has audit powers.

Another London university, stung by last year’s observation that its stated £12,500 postgraduate “minimum” was less than the sum of its own itemised breakdown, has raised the minimum to £14,500. Its own breakdown now sums to roughly £15,450 at the cheapest end. The correction preserved the contradiction and moved it £2,000 up the page – and added an unexplained “£75 a week” utilities line for good measure.

Sources: trust us

Where do the numbers come from? Mostly, nowhere. The modal sourcing across 141 providers is silence – figures presented as facts of nature. Where a method is described, it is often a job title – one Yorkshire university’s minimum costs have been “estimated by our support teams” since at least 2021, which makes those teams either clairvoyant or asleep – another’s “sector averages… monitored by our Student Money team” has been monitoring the same £3 TV licence for six years.

Where an external source is named, the news does not improve. The NatWest Student Living Index is enjoying a revival: one university crowns itself “the UK’s most affordable student city” on the strength of the 2025 edition; another lists the Index among the sources for its actual budget figures; a third builds its entire monthly breakdown on the August 2024 edition, citing a discredited survey a year late. It’s all twaddle – see here, here, here and here.

The withdrawn Which? student budget calculator – deleted years ago – is still recommended by name on several live pages, including a parents’ guide, presumably on the basis that parents enjoy heritage brands.

The compilation award goes to a blog post in north Wales, served under this year’s Clearing banner. Its sources: the NatWest Index (2021 edition), Save the Student (2022), and an accommodation platform (2023). Its content: private housing “can cost up to £266 per month” when “compared to that of £1300 in London – a 132% increase”, which is not what a rise from £266 to £1,300 is.

And the sector’s favourite source remains Save the Student’s annual money survey – a fine piece of work whose own headline findings are that students are skint, skip meals and use food banks. Universities strip those caveats and serve the spending averages as budget guidance – what hard-up students manage to spend, rebadged as what applicants should plan to spend.

One north-eastern institution simply relabelled the national survey table as its own students’ average monthly living costs and stamped it “08/07/24”, where it remains, two recruitment cycles later – the November 2025 capture is identical.

Cry regulation

Which brings us to the Office for Students’ proposed new condition C6 on treating students fairly – a consultation that closed last month, and to which the sector’s representative bodies have responded in a register I can only describe as wounded.

Universities UK supports fairness in principle but insists the OfS “should not seek to establish a higher regulatory standard than that required by existing consumer protection legislation”. University Alliance warns that the proposed condition “goes way beyond existing consumer protection law”, raises “serious questions about proportionality”, and might cause “increased risk aversion” – as though the sector’s current approach to cost information displayed a reckless excess of care.

And MillionPlus, while supporting transparency, cautions that the proposed publication requirements “will be a significant undertaking” and that information requirements “should remain focused on what students genuinely need”.

Well, what students need at the very least is an honest, dated, sourced estimate of what it will cost to live while they study, with a clear warning that past students often underspend, and inflation means those figures will rise during their course. Four in ten providers publish no estimate at all, while much of the rest publish archaeology.

Even better would be for the sector to get together and fund Loughborough University’s Centre for Research in Social Policy (CRSP) to update its Minimum Income Standard for students – which last year calculated that a student needs £61,000 for a minimum socially acceptable standard of living over the course of a three-year degree.

The sector says it can be trusted to treat students fairly without a new condition. Really? The universities that do this well prove it costs almost nothing. The rest have had four summers of being told, a consumer law framework the CMA refreshed in 2024, and the strongest possible incentive – their own recruitment – to get it right.

What they evidently need is a regulator prepared to read their websites the way an applicant does, and consequences when what’s written there isn’t true. If being required to publish an accurate number once a year is a “burden”, the word for what students have been carrying doesn’t appear in any consultation response.

The post The perfect storm: AI, assessment and a sector under pressure appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Ciaran Donaghy, Lead Policy Officer (Devolved Nations) and Rebecca Robinson, Data Analyst (Higher Education Insight), both of QAA.

Everyone’s talking about it – and has been doing so with increasing urgency over the last three years. From scandalised press commentators, anxious moral philosophers and concerned policymakers, through to lecturers, students, pedagogic experts, quality professionals and learning technologists, the impact of generative artificial intelligence on higher education has been one of the defining conversations of the sector in recent years.

It may therefore come as a surprise to those outside the sector to discover that there is no single response to the proliferation of GenAI tools in higher education. There are, of course, a range of institutional responses – and that variability is something to be expected in a sector that celebrates the diversity and autonomy of its institutions. But what our new State of the Nation report, The Perfect Storm: AI, assessment and a sector under pressure, finds is that the variability runs deeper than institutional differences. It runs through the practices of different academic departments, programmes, modules and individual practitioners within institutions, resulting in confusion among staff and students, and real inconsistencies in the learner experience.

GenAI continues to stymie the sector – and collectively, we’ve shied away from a comprehensive sector response, perhaps because it feels too big, too impossible to come up with an approach that accommodates all the various nuances and diversity higher education contains. Some variability is good and necessary. Adapting to subject content, assessment methods and student characteristics can serve learners well, and a sector in rapid transition in response to the challenges posed by GenAI is always going to be one in which practice is uneven. But where variability is driven, not by pedagogy, but by mismatched policies; lack of clarity for students; gaps in staff confidence and understanding; or differences in student access to and skills with AI tools, it becomes a fundamental risk to the conditions under which academic standards can be assured.

Our report examines and collates the findings of a range of recent studies of GenAI use in higher education and the issues and trends identified by QAA’s own review reports, alongside perspectives gleaned from a series of roundtables we held with student and sector staff stakeholders this spring.

The report identifies several key risks. There are real questions around the validity of assessment design when AI use can’t be reliably verified. There are concerns about foundational skills and about the meaning of a degree when some graduates may be achieving qualifications without engaging substantively with their studies. But perhaps the most striking finding is the gap between institutional policies and their implementation on the ground.

This gap matters because it falls hardest on students. Students experience the unevenness of policy implementation before they experience the policy itself, encountering different rules and expectations within a single programme of study, with uncertainties about what is permitted and anxieties about potential breaches of institutional policy. These inconsistencies and uncertainties may most significantly impact upon the experiences and outcomes of international students, students for whom English is a second language, neurodivergent students and students lacking cultural capital and technological confidence in the legitimate academic uses of this technology.

Our report therefore urges institutions to address consistency of student experience as a priority. This issue represented the single most recurring concern identified across our review evidence and our direct engagement with staff and students. Providers may therefore wish to consider how their policies are operationalised in practice, and how legitimate variation between disciplines and modules is communicated to students in ways that don’t produce confusion.

We are very aware of the resourcing constraints currently affecting our sector and that many institutional responses to the challenges posed by GenAI can, by virtue of their emphatically human focus, prove to be particularly resource-intensive. We are nevertheless recommending institutions ensure staff and students have the skills and confidence to use these tools and for students and staff to engage in any such training opportunities. Training emerged as the single strongest need flagged by both our staff and student roundtable groups – training focused not only on how to use GenAI, but on how to use it well, affording due consideration of the ethical, environmental and cognitive concerns it may raise.

We are also recommending that institutions should, from the outset, build student voice into the development of GenAI policy. Co-creation with students has repeatedly been identified as a feature of good practice in QAA reviews and was strongly endorsed by both our staff and student participants in our research.

title: Dons call for Cambridge leaders to take blame for Jason Arday appointment

full_text:
The University of Cambridge’s leaders deserve blame for the “grotesque racism unleashed” by Jason Arday’s appointment as professor, according to academics calling for the university to hold an independent inquiry.

The Guardian understands that senior dons at Cambridge are circulating a joint letter calling for an inquiry into the processes and circumstances around Arday being given the position, with many suggesting the university wanted a “quick fix” to improve the diversity of its staff.

Arday was appointed as professor of sociology of education in 2023 at the relatively young age of 37 and despite a slim track record of research and publications compared with those appointed to similar chairs at Cambridge.

Arday resigned on Wednesday after more than a week of public questions involving plagiarism in his PhD thesis and other publications, allegations of exaggerating his academic appointments, mounting controversy over his claims to have raised millions of pounds for charity, and lurid statements involving masked attackers and even a pig’s head delivered to his parents’ home in London.

Arday is preparing to publish his memoir in the US and UK in the coming days and told the Guardian that its publisher, Simon & Schuster, is to pay him “1.4 million” for his extraordinary backstory, which includes being unable to speak until he was 11 years old.

The group of Cambridge academics want any inquiry to include external members and be given independent status. They point to concerns over the appointment committee for Arday’s post, and to previous disputes within the university’s faculty of education where Arday was based.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge’s English faculty and one of the group organising the letter, said: “An independent investigation must scrutinise how such an early-career appointment to a very senior and prestigious professorial chair was made and what both the faculty of education and university management may have got very badly wrong.”

She added: “Whatever the results of any investigation, the university bears no little responsibility for the grotesque racism which this whole business has unleashed, and for the harm done both to the individual in the line of fire, to Black academics as a group, and the broader field of critical race studies.

“This requires accountability now from those responsible, not a cover-up.”

Other academics who spoke to the Guardian said they had been surprised by Arday’s appointment in 2023, with one sociologist admitting to never having heard of Arday before: “When it was announced I looked for his body of work, and it was disappointing to say the least.”

Gopal said Cambridge had been too tempted to “cut corners on the hard work of fostering equality and inclusion” by opting for a media-friendly appointment.

“The extent to which this appointment was paraded in the media by the university … raises questions about whether the university sought public kudos for itself rather than teaching and research from this appointment.

“It is highly unusual, to say the least, to appoint such an early-career academic to a very senior post,” Gopal said.

“Academic misconduct also needs more robust and transparent procedures in place, as more than one case at Cambridge indicates.

“The university must also pay attention to the consequences of putting young people of colour in highly visible places to carry the burden of representation before they are ready to withstand scrutiny.”

When the controversy first erupted, the university briefed journalists that it stood by its appointment process, and publicly defended Arday as “the victim of a vile campaign” to discredit him.

But on Wednesday night the university abruptly announced that it would open a fresh investigation after receiving “new information” about his qualifications and appointments.

Shortly afterwards Arday said he would resign, adding: “I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgment.”

The university and other organisations have since distanced themselves from Arday by deleting webpages and excising references, which one academic described as “wiping away the traces”.

Jesus College, Cambridge, and the university’s faculty of education have taken down Arday’s staff profiles.

Arday had signed up to speakers’ bureaus and, since his Cambridge appointment, has addressed a number of commercial organisations, including the annual conference of the Association of British Insurers in 2025.

Simon & Schuster’s speakers bureau lists Arday as “an internationally sought-after speaker for industry conferences, corporate events, university lectures, and more, and has travelled across the United States for speaking engagements”.

In 2024 Arday was a keynote speaker at US National Association of Funeral Directors international convention in New Orleans. His subsequent appearances, however, may dry up: an appearance in Arizona promised for October this year has also been removed.

full_text:
Danish teenagers will have to make an oral defence of their written essays to combat AI cheating, the government has announced.

Pupils aged 16 to 19 at upper secondary school (known in Denmark as gymnasiet) will also be encouraged to do written assignments at school under controlled conditions, including monitoring of their computer screens, rather than at home.

The measures, announced on Thursday as pupils prepare to go back to school next week after the summer break, will come into immediate effect after Magnus Heunicke, the country’s education minister, demanded urgent action.

“Unfortunately, we have a problem with AI cheating in upper secondary schools,” he said. “Action is needed now.”

AI had posed a growing challenge to teaching and exams, the education ministry said. It is hoped the new measures will help to establish clearer guidelines for when pupils are not permitted to use it.

The government is also preparing a comprehensive national strategy for AI use in all schools and the wider education sector.

Heunicke said he would speak to schools, teachers and students to “ensure that AI does not undermine students’ competencies, professionalism and, not least, the ability to think for themselves”.

The first measure to be introduced is the oral defence of exam assignments written at home. About 9,000 upper secondary school students each year write a big assignment (known as større skriftlige opgave or SSO), which they will now have to defend orally. The ministry said it would speak to schools about the best way to do this.

Upper secondary schools will also be required to use monitoring tools to oversee how computers are being used for written exams. They are required to install firewalls to filter what is available on the school network during exams and teaching.

The third measure is a plea to schools to encourage pupils to do more of their written assignments at school under controlled conditions, to “follow the students’ work process, provide relevant feedback and create a more accurate basis for assessment”.

The ready availability of AI tools is upending education around the world for teachers and pupils, leaving governments scrambling to assess if and how they should intervene.

In neighbouring Sweden, a study found that the number of students suspended or warned for unauthorised AI use rose by 688% between 2023 and 2025. The government has commissioned a review into how schools are tackling AI cheating, which will report back in April.

Announcing the review, Lotta Edholm, the Swedish minister for upper secondary school, said in January: “There is no reason to turn a blind eye to cheating students. Cheating is completely unacceptable regardless of what form. It risks affecting grades that should reflect students’ knowledge and in the long term, students are not actually learning what they should.”

title: Serious questions for Cambridge after professor at centre of plagiarism row resigns
summary: Jason Arday’s resignation poses questions about standards and a push for diversity, writes education editor Branwen Jeffreys.
full_text:
The University of Cambridge is facing serious questions about its academic standards and push for diversity after its youngest black professor resigned amid allegations of copying other academics' research.

Jason Arday's appointment in 2023 was hailed at the time as a progressive moment. Now, Cambridge says it has launched an investigation after "new information" emerged about his academic qualifications and honorary appointments.

There are two fundamental questions for the university.

Did it fail to adequately check Arday's credentials when appointing him, and did it defend that decision because of an institutional push to position itself as more diverse?

For one of the world's leading universities known for academic excellence and globally significant research, this is about its institutional culture and decision-making at the highest level.

The biggest reputational risk surrounds the accusations of academic plagiarism now under investigation - and denied by Arday - because they get to the heart of what a university is about.

The University of Cambridge uses the common definition of plagiarism as "passing off someone else's work as if it were your own without appropriate acknowledgement".

There is no allegation more serious that can be levelled at an academic.

One of the fundamental purposes of a research-led university is the creation of knowledge through original thinking, insights and inquiry.

The quality of this is the foundation of Cambridge's reputation, and a source of significant funding.

Arday did not start his university journey at an elite institution.

He has a degree from the University of Surrey in education studies and physical education, a master's from St Mary's University in London, and a PhD in education awarded by Liverpool John Moores University.

The reason the PhD has attracted so much attention is because it is the first major piece of original research anyone wanting a career as an academic must complete.

Arday's critics claim that his work relied on copying other academics without properly crediting their work from the outset, which he denies.

He went on to become an associate professor at Durham University and professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow.

In other words, there is a line of institutions behind Cambridge now facing similar questions about their appointment processes.

The entire higher education system relies on accepting the qualifications awarded by another institution in good faith. Regulation and standards are meant to create a common currency.

That has now unravelled with what began as a blog a couple of years ago escalating in recent weeks, with more journalists unpicking aspects of Arday's life story and asking questions.

It is at this point Cambridge faces questions about whether it was defending its own reputation as much as an individual academic.

Just a couple of weeks ago, the university was briefing journalists that this was a campaign against a black academic, its appointment system was rigorous, and it would be robustly defended.

So why might Cambridge have had a blind spot that delayed an investigation which could settle the matter?

The university has spent the last decade working to redress the perception that the institution is a bastion of affluent white privilege.

Roger Mosey, the former master of the university's Selwyn College, said Arday's academic background was "unconventional" for a Cambridge professor, but that his life story as an autistic man who said he could not read until he was 18 was what had seemingly "made him a compelling candidate".

Equality, diversity and inclusion are reasonable goals for a leading university, Mosey wrote in the Times, but risk becoming contentious "when they are baked into inflexible policies and questionable appointment processes".

Part of the answer may also lie in how black academics feel in general as part of a tiny minority in the wider university community.

In the last academic year, only 75 of Cambridge's 6,180 academics at all levels were identified as black, according to the Higher Education Statistics Authority (HESA).

If you look at professors across the UK, 270 are identified as black out of a total of more than 26,000, according to HESA definitions - around 1%.

The University and College Union has previously highlighted an ethnicity pay gap and called for it to be redressed. It declined to comment on this case.

Both Cambridge and Oxford have faced sustained scrutiny over their whiteness as institutions, with vocal critics over the last 15 years including the MP David Lammy.

He extracted data from the universities showing how few offers were made to black students despite the number being awarded top A-Level grades which would potentially qualify them for a place.

In 2018, Cambridge said it needed help to attract more talented black students, and unexpectedly the rapper Stormzy answered the call by setting up a scholarship to encourage students to apply.

Although the support was for a handful of students, it was a reputational coup for the university - allowing it to position itself as a more open and inclusive institution.

Now it will have to balance the potential reputational fall out of the Jason Arday row for its academic credibility, with how that might be perceived by future talented black students and academics.

title: The 'education gap' hiding behind picture-perfect Cornwall and Devon
summary: Behind the South West's postcard image, poverty and isolation are limiting opportunities for many young people.
full_text:
This year, millions of holidaymakers will head to Cornwall and Devon for their sandy beaches and pretty coastal towns - just two reasons why the South West peninsula is England's top tourist destination.

Yet behind its wild coastal beauty and affluent towns lies a different story: one of lost opportunities and the unfulfilled potential of many growing up in the region.

On almost every measure, the region is among the weakest educationally, according to the South West Social Mobility Commission, a coalition of organisations trying to bring about change.

Disparities in GCSE results are often framed through the lens of a North-South divide, but that narrative can obscure the challenges facing children in coastal and rural parts of England.

When you look at the regional data for English and maths GCSE passes for all pupils in England, you can see that, overall, the South outperforms the North.

Tanya Ovenden-Hope, Professor of Education at Plymouth Marjon University, describes what happens in the South West as "pretty poverty", and says this leads to fewer young people reaching their full potential.

She calls growing up in "poverty in a deprived coastal rural community a potentially toxic combination" for future life chances.

The government does measure the level of disadvantage in communities but Prof Ovenden-Hope says too much of that is done using measures that work for towns and cities, including transport.

"If you live in Cornwall you have to own a car. It's not a luxury, it's a necessity, because everything you do and everywhere you go involves some kind of travel. That's not measured by the government's measures of deprivation."

This matters because it helps decide how government money is allocated across England.

"It's not all ice creams and sandy beaches and turquoise seas," says Dominic Wilkes, a headteacher who moved from Greater Manchester to Bude in North Cornwall.

Higher housing costs and the need for a car impact training and teacher recruitment. While the remoteness of some communities can also act as a deterrent for young teachers to move here from other parts of England, according to recent research.

For Wilkes, who works at the only secondary school in Bude, the main upside is better teacher retention, which helps build a deep connection to the local community.

But inspiring children to think about different options for their future comes with its challenges.

As a teacher in Greater Manchester, Wilkes could hop on a tram to take pupils to museums and different workplaces, including the BBC at MediaCity in Salford, as part of the curriculum.

The nearest railway station is about 30 miles from Budehaven Community School. Pupils travel in from scattered villages and the area offers a relatively limited range of employers able to broaden their horizons or spark ambitions beyond the classroom.

Year 10 pupil Ethan, from Budehaven Community School, wants to become a marine biologist and recently completed a work experience placement at a seal sanctuary that was a three-hour round trip by car.

"I love being in the sea and just protecting its habitats and wildlife, it really makes me excited to do something like that," he said.

"I think Cornwall's amazing and all my family are here but I think I want to be able to grow as a person. I think I can only do that by leaving and exploring new adventures."

Year 9 student Burt told us he had to travel to Oxfordshire and Coventry to take part in the National Youth Choir, which meant his dad had to book a hotel to break up the journey.

He thinks there are good opportunities to be found but they're more difficult, and sometimes costly, to access from his town.

But others told us Cornwall is the perfect location for them. Poppy wants to be a florist and dreams of opening a seasonal business selling homegrown local wildflowers.

Wilkes has decided to spend above average on careers advice and trips, including to universities, to help expand pupils' horizons but it is still hard.

He had to turn down an offer of work experience from a "brilliant company" because although it didn't look too far on a map, it was five hours each way by road, without a direct bus service.

This kind of challenge potentially deepens the divide between families who have the money to afford petrol for long-distance trips or holidays abroad, and those who are just about managing the basics with a rising cost of living.

In the South West, much of the local employment is in farming or tourism, with young adults looking to leave and build their careers elsewhere.

In 2024, jobs related to the visitor economy made up approximately 20% of employment in Cornwall.

The South West Social Mobility Commission has other concerns about children who receive free school meals in the region.

It warns that 46% of secondary pupils (and 27% of primary pupils) are persistently absent, which means missing 10% of their school time.

While suspensions, exclusions and home education are also among the highest in England "raising important questions about school engagement, belonging and access to education".

In young adulthood, the potential impact can be seen in the proportion who go on to university, one of the biggest long-term drivers of improved earnings and life chances between generations.

In the South West, 19% of those who grew up receiving free school meals go on to get a degree, the lowest level in England, and below the North East. The national average is 29%.

This is what motivated Nick Wakeling, a teacher at Colyton Grammar School, to get in touch.

He runs the Colyton Foundation, a charity that supports young people into university.

One of the foundation's schemes is Your Future Story, backed by schools and universities to support 1,000 secondary school pupils from lower income families through to university with targeted support.

Libby is now considering a creative degree after Your Future Story arranged for her to go on a trip to Falmouth, a 1 hour 40 minute drive away. It "gave me an idea of what university would be like," she says.

There is a big push for locally generated solutions from the South West Social Mobility Commission, funded by a coalition including Exeter University, which warns the region is near the bottom on most measures of educational attainment from early childhood onwards.

While this can limit life chances in terms of getting to higher earnings, fewer young people in the South West are not in education, employment or training than most other parts of England. This is at a time when the national concern about what are called NEETs has reached an all-time high.

The report found the South West has the highest proportion of people who received free school meals as children in sustained work by the age of 28.

A Department for Education Spokesperson said: "This government believes every child should grow up with opportunity on their doorstep and hope for the future, with an education system that opens doors and cuts the link between background and success."

From this September, two pilot projects on raising education results in coastal areas are getting under way in Hastings and Scarborough in what the government is calling Mission Coastal.

The hope is to find approaches that transfer elsewhere, but the more rural and coastal South West may need to find quite different solutions.

Additional reporting by Isobel Cottam and Libby Rogers.

title: Self-Reflecting to Teach with More Cultural Responsiveness
summary:
Many college teachers want to respond to students’ identities and cultures with respect, accurate perceptions, and sensitivity. We may face challenges within ourselves that arise from being shaped by societal forces. A self-reflective, repeating process of “…awareness, analysis, action, and accountability” (The Adaway Group; Love 2010) helped me. I hope that sharing my experiences with this process can help college teachers already engaged in similar processes or those who want to try something new in order to become even more culturally responsive with their students.   Awareness […]

The post Self-Reflecting to Teach with More Cultural Responsiveness appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
Many college teachers want to respond to students’ identities and cultures with respect, accurate perceptions, and sensitivity. We may face challenges within ourselves that arise from being shaped by societal forces. A self-reflective, repeating process of “…awareness, analysis, action, and accountability” (The Adaway Group; Love 2010) helped me. I hope that sharing my experiences with this process can help college teachers already engaged in similar processes or those who want to try something new in order to become even more culturally responsive with their students.

Awareness: Self-reflecting on my teaching and interactions with students to become aware of how my biases and identity could be affecting them.

Analysis: Thinking through what I discover to see what is going on and “pivoting from problem to possibility” with the help of supportive colleagues. Thinking of ways to try to reduce the negative effects of my biases and identity on students.

Accountability: Asking for help from supportive colleagues of different cultures and identities from myself to see my blind spots.

Action: Acting on those new ways of teaching.

Awareness

My first step was to make regular time to reflect on my teaching and my interactions with students, using these questions, informed by the Illinois State Board of Education Culturally Responsive Teaching and Leading Standard A:

What happened in my teaching and interaction(s) with student(s)?

What ideas and biases motivated my actions?

How might my identity have affected my perspectives and beliefs about students?

How might my biases and perceptions have impacted students?

What are ways to mitigate my bias and/or negative impact on students?

I made a list of some aspects of my identity and some of my probable biases to spark my reflections. Reviewing this list provided me a more defined path to follow:

Race/ethnicity: White/non-Hispanic

National Origin: United Stated of America

Language: English (home language)

Sex and gender: Cis-gendered woman

Sexual orientation: Heterosexual

Physical ability: Able with experience of temporary disability

Developmental ability: Development of sense of self

Emotional ability: Strong student of this

Socioeconomic class: Middle class (maybe upper middle class)

Religion: Christian/Lutheran

My probable biases:

Racism

Classism

Sexism

Homophobia

Unearned privilege (white privilege)

Eurocentrism

Ableism

Here is an example of a self-reflection about my socioeconomic status and probable classism:

“I am not sure if this is about my identity or my biases or both: I noticed that I had internal negative reactions to how some students dressed for in-class presentations in a first-year education class. This is a diverse class of students from Latine, Black, and white backgrounds Several Black and Latine students revealed skin on their torsos and/or wore short shorts. I wondered if that is a way of dressing that they experience as dressing up. It is very different from my experience. I am also aware that as a teacher educator who teaches field experience courses where students go into classrooms in schools, I do talk with students in those classes about what is considered to be professional attire. I do not do this in classes that do not have this field component like this one. I am aware as I reflect that I associate this way of students dressing with attire for going to a night club and/or being sexually provocative.”

When I reflected on the impact that I may have had on students, I wrote:

“I may have looked askance at them, unconsciously expressing my negative judgment about their appearance. I can see that this could have impacted them negatively: they may have sensed some disapproval from me. If they did, this may have negatively affected their confidence in making their presentations.”

Analysis

I shared with supportive colleagues (in the Writers’ Collective of the Center for Success in High Needs Schools) how discouraging it was to discover this and other ways that my perceptions and biases may have negatively affected my students. They helped me “pivot” from “problem to possibility” by telling me about their own and Dr. Shawn A. Ginwright’s work (Ginwright, 2022). Ginwright writes, “…our job is to lean into the practice of possibilities and strive for the future we want to create.” (p. 179)

Colleagues Dr. Gloria McDaniel-Hall and Dr. Ava Belisle-Chatterjee shared their blog “Let’s Pivot for Change” where they discuss with blog visitors ways to reimagine justice and ourselves. When I felt down about what I was discovering in myself, I chose to put my energies into finding ways to reduce the effects of my biases on students.

Analysis, Accountability, and Action

In another example of my pivot from problem to possibility, when a proposal to present my self-reflective process at a conference was not accepted, I chose to use the reviewers’ questions to improve my process. They asked:

“How is doing reflective work limited by whiteness?”

“What role, if any, do other white people or people of color play in this reflective process?”

“How do you know what your own socialization and/or knowledge base is limiting you from being able to reflect upon?”

I shared these questions with colleagues in the Writing Collective along with my reservations about asking for help from people of color. I explained that I did not want to ask people of color to do the work that I needed to do as a white person in uncovering my biases and reducing their effects. Some colleagues there were generous in their offers to talk with me.

Through a conversation we had, I see now that in order to mitigate my bias about students’ attire, I need to learn more about the ways in which what is considered to be professional is problematic and how professionalism can be considered as being equivalent to whiteness.

As a result of this conversation, I saw the importance of talking with students in all of my courses about the importance of doing what they can to be seen as professional in order to gain and keep professional positions and the problematic aspects of professionalism. In my current teaching, I am in the process of doing both with students.

Another example of my engagement in this multi-step process of self-reflection uncovered that my identity as able and white affected my perception of a student with a disability. As I worked to understand what was going on in myself, I saw that I minimized the effect of this disability on this student of color and their experience of school. I was unaware of what it could mean to an elementary student to be closely monitored by the school nurse in a classroom where the classroom teacher responded to this student by underestimating this student’s academic capabilities. For the rest of the semester, I tried to be very aware of this bias and allow the student to express her experience even more freely than I may have before then.

Conclusion

Responding to students’ cultures and identities with more accurate, respectful, and sensitive perceptions requires reflecting on our own identities and biases and how they can lead to our doing otherwise. This multi-step process of self-reflection has helped me:

Recognize how my perceptions of students are influenced by my identity

Notice how I act out my unconscious biases in my interactions with students

Ask for help to see my blind spots caused by my socialization and knowledge base from supportive colleagues with cultures and identities different from mine

Use my discoveries to enact ways of doing things differently and reducing the negative effects of my biases on students

What fuels my efforts is the possibility of creating a more culturally responsive learning environment in my classroom where the people I teach can be more free to be and become their wonderful, authentic selves, less hindered by my misperceptions and biases about their cultures and identities.

Dr. Elizabeth Meadows teaches a diverse population of undergraduate and graduate students in teacher preparation and related fields at Roosevelt University in Chicago and Schaumburg, Illinois. In her current research, she reflects on her own identity, motivations, and biases and their impacts on her teaching and on her students. Meadows’ main purpose in this research is to further her ongoing, anti-bias, and culturally responsive efforts as a white teacher educator to build and maintain learning environments, including her teacher-student relationships with students, that are most conducive for all future teachers of all cultures and identities whom she teaches. Another purpose is to publish her research in order to contribute to the literature on self-reflective, anti-bias efforts by teacher educators.

References and Resources:

The Adaway Group https://adawaygroup.com/

The blog and community forum by Dr. Ava Belisle Chatterjee and Dr. Gloria McDaniel-Hall called “Let’s Pivot for Change” https://pivotforchange.wixsite.com/connect

Ginwright, S. (2022). The Four Pivots: Reimagining Ourselves, Reimagining Justice. North Atlantic Books.

Illinois State Board of Education Culturally Responsive Teaching and Leading Standards https://www.isbe.net/Pages/Culturally-Responsive-Teaching-Leading-Standards.aspx

Love, B. (2010). Developing a liberatory consciousness. In M. Adams, W. J. Blumenfeld, C. R. Castañeda, H. W. Hackman, M. L. Peters, & X. Zúñiga (Eds.), Readings for diversity and social justice (2nd ed., pp. 50–58). Routledge.

title: Higher Ed IT Budgets Face a Dual Threat: Federal Research Cuts and State Funding Pressure
summary:
Higher education leadership and IT teams are battling ghost students, establishing AI governance and managing competing priorities as students return to campus. Adding to this strain is a major shift in federal philosophy about National Institutes of Health grants, National Science Foundation funding and broader federal research funding cuts in what has historically been a university-centric system. 
In previous years, Congress has approved the federal budget, so that agencies such as NIH, NSF and the Department of Energy’s Office of Science could move swiftly to release funding…
full_text:
NIH and NSF Funding Cuts Are Hitting Higher Ed IT From Every Direction

This announcement and its possible implications aren’t the only issues higher ed is facing. The dual budget crisis is compounded by state funding cuts and the long-feared enrollment cliff deficits arriving simultaneously.

Hiring freezes, competition with private sector salaries to retain talent, and the struggle to balance infrastructure and network modernization with depleted budgets and lean staffing are just a few of the difficulties higher ed IT leadership are already dealing with.

“Roughly speaking, IT organizations are somewhere in the neighborhood of 5% of the total budget of the university,” says John Rathje, a CDW strategist and former vice president and CIO of Kent State University. “Let's say we have a $100 million budget. That means IT has $5 million. And if IT can save 10%, that means IT saves half a million dollars. What about the other 95%?”

On April 30, Kent State University President Todd Diacon announced the layoffs of 45 employees to help offset a projected $18 million shortfall for the Ohio university.

State funding for higher ed nationally saw a 4% increase in 2025 — which is just 2% when adjusted for inflation — with 17 states seeing a decrease from the previous year, according to the National Education Association’s NEA Higher Ed State Funding Report.

Due to a significant decline in out-of-state, first-year student enrollment, University of Oregon President Karl Scholz announced in May that the institution would need to cut $65 million from its budget, beyond last year’s $30 million cut. He noted in an announcement to faculty that “roughly 80 percent of our Education & General Fund budget comes from tuition revenue.”

“I believe we are now at a crossroads. We could take smaller steps matching short-run expenses with revenues. But with smaller actions, we would have little confidence that we would not have to make another round of cuts next year,” Scholz noted. “The university community has gone through budget cuts multiple times in recent years. That is a dynamic that produces a great deal of pain while failing to produce clear, long-term solutions to address root causes.”

Facing a projected $1.5 billion state budget shortfall, the Board of Governors of the Colorado State University System announced that it had approved a systemwide strategy to keep tuition levels low for its students — a challenging balancing act with rising mandatory costs.

“Colorado’s fiscal reality is requiring thoughtful and often difficult choices across higher education, and our campuses are no different,” said Chancellor Tony Frank in a CSU announcement. “We appreciate the state’s continued investment and choice to keep tuition increases modest, although flat funding in the face of rising costs still presents real challenges. In addition, uncertainty around federal research support is constraining institutions to plan conservatively while staying focused on our core mission of access, student success, and impact for the state.”

How Federal Research Funding Cuts Are Straining University IT Infrastructure

Large institutions usually run separate IT operations for administrative functions and research computing, with the research side serving the scientific mission, federal compliance requirements and other needs. Typically, research computing labs have built stand-alone, localized infrastructure funded largely by huge federal grants.

With agencies capping critical Facilities & Administrative indirect cost reimbursements at 15% (down from historical 60% averages), universities are losing tens of millions of dollars annually.

“There are formulas that take a single pie and start slicing that pie up, so that pie typically never gets bigger,” says Rathje. “However, external forces do get bigger, so the cost of goods and labor continues to rise.”

The bottom line: Regardless of where the cuts originated, higher education leadership and IT teams will have to confront the shortfall.

“Staffing has been impacted most in the research area for the larger research institutions,” says Barajas-Murphy. “But now we’re going to see if that the funding for facilities, research centers — things that are on campuses — is going to shift, and by how much.”

Rightsizing Cloud and HPC When Funding Disappears

“I think the big thing is to know what you’re trying to deliver to the mission,” says Rathje. “And then have the right set of tools — not three sets of tools. That’s part one. Part two is to architect those tools in a way that gives the university the capability to improve its outcomes and perhaps generate revenue through scale. The tools could also be used to maybe reduce cost, friction and waste within the organization.”

University IT leaders are now charged with identifying which high-computing environments will be most impacted by the lack of grant support — while cloud spending continues to outpace university tuition growth — and examining how turning to FinOps might help them merge research metadata with fiscal data to create centralized governance models.

Some universities are already experiencing the impact of rightsizing. Johns Hopkins University has historically been the largest recipient of federal research funding among U.S. universities. The Baltimore institution laid off more than 100 employees in June after its federal research portfolio dropped by more than $500 million last year, as “these downward trends have continued unabated” into 2026, President Ron Daniels said in a message to the university community.

“As our federal research portfolio shrinks, the infrastructure around it must change in parallel,” a university spokesperson shared with press.

EXPLORE: Data-driven spending decisions improve efficiency for higher ed IT teams.

This pattern is playing out at research institutions across the country. In a May video address, Massachusetts Institute of Technology President Sally Kornbluth said the funding picture is still concerning even after Congress partially restored agency budgets.

“Compared to this time last year, MIT has experienced a decline in campus research activity funded by federal awards of more than 20%,” says Kornbluth.

Considering all funding sources, sponsored research activity at MIT is now 10% less than a year ago, and new graduate student enrollments (outside of the institution’s business school and an engineering program) are down by nearly 20% for next year.

Managed Services as a Budget Bridge

“Managed services could become a very foundational part of an organization’s response, allowing them to focus on best values for their labor investments,” says Rathje. “Rather than having a team member for everything that they do, maybe they focus their teams on the real value-add items, and they look to a managed service to cover other things and do some cost predictability around that.”

Modernization is still top of mind with most higher ed IT leaders, with 92% of respondents to a 2025 EDUCAUSE QuickPoll reporting that their institution is either considering modernization or has already modernized some systems.

“However, the path to data modernization in higher education is complex, with only 1% of respondents indicating they feel their institution has fully modernized its data management and strategy,” the report states.

One option when roles tied to grants disappear: Universities can turn to creative solutions with managed services and their vendors to keep research systems running while rebuilding internal capacity.

DISCOVER: Cost-effective risk management approaches for your higher ed IT team.

“Forward-looking CIO and senior IT leaders who are making these purchasing decisions are looking at the purchasing process to implement things like staff augmentation, inclusive of a training component,” says Barajas-Murphy. “From the conversations I’m seeing, CIOs increasingly are looking at procurement and purchasing and considering such questions as, how can we nest-in training?”

Some CIOs are already looking at how to embed these solutions into their procurement processes through staff augmentation.

The dual-budget pressure of the OSTP announcement, along with enrollment declines and the state funding picture, isn’t a storm to wait out.
